summary.en: Assign exam slots with exact m-colouring, then compare its guarantee with a fast greedy colouring.
summary.bn: গ্রাফে সংঘাত থাকলে আলাদা পরীক্ষার স্লট দাও, আর exact সার্চের সঙ্গে greedy পদ্ধতি মিলিয়ে দেখো।

notes: The demonstrated programs use C17; the lesson states their input and arithmetic bounds.

sections.title: Colour a fixed prefix of vertices
Search a palette before changing it
Compare a rejected and accepted colour
A witness and an exhaustion proof
A greedy miss is not impossibility
A small fixed matrix in C17

examples.title: Decide whether the exam slots suffice
examples.explanationHtml: The exact program reads a palette size. Three slots yield A:1, B:2, C:3, D:1, E:2. Two slots produce Impossible after exhaustive search. The fixed graph keeps the search small enough to follow.

examples.title: Colour greedily in vertex order
examples.explanationHtml: The greedy program assigns the first safe colour among one through five. It reports three slots for this order. It does not claim the result is optimal on every graph or every ordering.

examples.title: Count labelled triangle colourings
examples.explanationHtml: The final program tries every palette assignment to three pairwise adjacent vertices. For three colours it reports six assignments. Relabelling colours produces different assignments here, even though all six share the same structural pattern.

practice.title: Schedule the fixed conflict graph
practice.statementHtml:

hints: Keep the state convention and stopping rule described in Graph Colouring.

practice.title: Count triangle colour assignments
practice.statementHtml:
Input: Palette size for a triangle (1..5):

Output: Print the prompt, then Labelled colourings: for a triangle.
hints: Keep the state convention and stopping rule described in Graph Colouring.
Backtracking decides whether a fixed palette is sufficient.

practice.title: Explain why the fixed exam graph needs at least three slots.
practice.statementHtml: Explain why the fixed exam graph needs at least three slots.
hints: Begin with the state and the input conditions.
practice.answerHtml: A, B and C form a triangle, so each pair conflicts. They require three different colours. Assigning [1,2,3,1,2] satisfies the remaining CD and DE conflicts, proving three slots suffice.

practice.title: Give a vertex order where greedy colouring of a bipartite path uses three colours.
practice.statementHtml: Give a vertex order where greedy colouring of a bipartite path uses three colours.
hints: Begin with the state and the input conditions.
practice.answerHtml: For path 0-1-2-3, use order 0,3,1,2. Greedy assigns 1 to 0, 1 to 3, 2 to 1, then 3 to 2 because its neighbours have colours 2 and 1. The path still has a two-colouring [1,2,1,2].

quiz.prompt: What does a proper graph colouring forbid?
quiz.explanation: Only endpoints connected by a conflict edge must differ.

quiz.prompt: What does failure of one greedy ordering prove about m-colourability?
options: That ordering did not find an m-colouring
quiz.explanation: Greedy failure gives no general impossibility proof; backtracking explores alternatives.

quiz.prompt: How many colours must a triangle use?
quiz.explanation: Its three vertices are pairwise adjacent, requiring three distinct colours.

quiz.prompt: Why does allowed(v,c) inspect only earlier vertices in the exact solver?
options: Only earlier vertices have committed colours
quiz.explanation: Future choices are tested when they become current vertices.

quiz.prompt: What real-world condition should create an exam conflict edge?
options: Two courses share a title prefix
A student must attend both exams
quiz.explanation: A shared student cannot attend both courses at the same time.

quiz.prompt: Which graph cannot be properly coloured for any palette size?
quiz.explanation: A self-loop would require a vertex to differ from itself.

quiz.prompt: Which upper bound follows from first-fit greedy colouring on a simple graph?
quiz.explanation: At most the degree many colours are forbidden by earlier neighbours, leaving one among degree plus one.

quiz.prompt: How many proper labelled three-colour assignments does this triangle search count?
quiz.explanation: Three distinct colour labels can be assigned in 3*2*1 ways.

quiz.prompt: Does edge AB accept the equal endpoint colours in this certificate?
quiz.explanation: Equal labels violate the edge, so the validity expression is zero.

quiz.prompt: Which first-fit colour is chosen when neighbour colours one and two are forbidden?
quiz.explanation: The first unused positive colour is three.

keyPoints.bn: পাশাপাশি যুক্ত ভার্টেক্সে আলাদা কালার দিতে হয়।

keyPoints.en: Backtracking decides whether a fixed palette is sufficient.
keyPoints.bn: নির্দিষ্ট কয়টা কালার দিয়ে হবে কি না, ব্যাকট্র্যাকিং তা বের করে।

keyPoints.en: Undo a failed colour before trying another choice.
keyPoints.bn: একটা কালারে কাজ না হলে সেটা সরিয়ে পরেরটা দেখো।

keyPoints.bn: greedy কালারিংয়ের ফল ভার্টেক্সের ক্রমের ওপর নির্ভর করে।

examQuestions.question: State the invariant and justify the time and space costs of Graph Colouring.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
The exact-search invariant is that assigned vertices form a proper colouring and future vertices are unassigned. The empty prefix satisfies it. The allowed test checks every new edge to an earlier endpoint, so accepting a candidate preserves it.

At a complete prefix, every edge has been checked when its later endpoint was assigned. The retained assignment is therefore proper. To show completeness, take any valid m-colouring. Its colour at each vertex is among the loop choices and conflicts with no earlier neighbour. The search eventually follows that sequence unless it has already found another valid witness.

If every branch fails, no valid m-colouring remains unexplored. Reporting failure is then a proof of impossibility within this finite model. A single unsuccessful greedy pass has no such guarantee because it never revisits its early choices.

Greedy colouring is still correct as a construction when it may introduce new colours. Each new vertex avoids all colours on earlier neighbours. Later neighbours will avoid its colour in turn. Thus the result is proper, though its colour count may exceed the minimum.

A full m-ary assignment tree has m^V leaves. For m>=2, it has O(m^V) total candidate edges up to a constant depending on that branching factor. Our adjacency-matrix safety test scans at most V earlier vertices per candidate, giving O(V*m^V) time as a conservative bound.

For m=1 the tree degenerates to a chain. Scanning earlier entries over all levels costs O(V^2) rather than interpreting the exponential expression too literally. The demonstration reserves a V-by-V matrix and O(V) colour and recursion storage. Its auxiliary search state is linear, separate from the input matrix.

The presented greedy routine may try up to V colours at each vertex and scan up to V neighbours for each trial. Its straightforward worst-case bound is O(V^3). A better implementation marks forbidden neighbour colours once per vertex, then finds the smallest unmarked colour. With a matrix that takes O(V^2) total work; adjacency lists can reduce neighbour scanning.

For a simple graph with maximum degree Delta, first-fit uses at most Delta+1 colours. At most Delta earlier neighbours can forbid colours, so one among the first Delta+1 remains available. This is an upper bound, not a statement that every graph requires that many colours.
